n: Jonathan, full of faith, proposes to his armor-bearer that they cross over to the Philistine outpost. He doesn't tell his father.

f.w: the young man that bare his armour
f.g: his armor-bearer, a trusted attendant who carried weapons and fought beside his master

n: Meanwhile Saul sits passively under a pomegranate tree at the edge of Gibeah with his six hundred men — a contrast with Jonathan's bold action.

f.g: A place near Gibeah; possibly a threshing floor area.

n: With Saul is Ahiah, a priest descended from Eli, wearing the ephod used to seek God's will. The mention of Eli's line reminds us of that house's doomed future. No one knows Jonathan has left.

f.g: Probably the same as Ahimelech, priest at Nob.
Here the high priest's garment, which held the Urim and Thummim used to inquire of the Lord.

n: The path across the ravine runs between two rocky cliffs, named Bozez and Seneh.

f.g: Possibly “shining” or “slippery.”
Possibly “thorny,” like a thorn bush.

n: One cliff faces north toward Michmash, the other south toward Gibeah. The geography makes clear how difficult and dangerous the climb is.
Jonathan states his faith: perhaps the Lord will act for us, because nothing can stop God from saving, whether by many or by few. Compare Gideon's three hundred.

f.g: A term for the Philistines as outsiders to God's covenant.

f.w: there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few

n: The armor-bearer pledges total loyalty: “I am with you, heart and soul.”

f.g: with you all the way, of one mind with you

n: Jonathan plans to show themselves to the Philistines openly.

f.g: reveal ourselves, let ourselves be seen

n: He sets a sign: if the Philistines say “wait there,” they will stay put.
But if the Philistines say “come up,” it will be the Lord's sign that He has given them victory. Jonathan seeks God's will before acting.

f.w: this shall be a sign unto us

n: When the two appear, the Philistines mock them as Hebrews crawling out of their holes — a jab at the Israelites hiding in caves.

f.w: the holes where they had hid themselves

n: The guards taunt, “Come up and we'll show you something!” — exactly the sign. Jonathan confidently tells his armor-bearer to follow, for the Lord has given them the victory.
Jonathan scrambles up the cliff on hands and feet. Then the Philistines fall before him, and his armor-bearer finishes them off.
In that first strike the two men kill about twenty Philistines in a small area, about half an acre.

f.g: Roughly half the area a pair of oxen could plow in a day.

n: Panic sweeps the entire Philistine army, and the earth itself shakes. The Hebrew suggests a “trembling of God” — the Lord Himself sent terror among them.

f.g: Literally “a trembling of God,” meaning a terror sent by God.

n: Saul's lookouts at Gibeah see the huge Philistine army falling apart, men scattering in every direction.

f.g: dissolved, scattered

n: Saul calls for a headcount and discovers that Jonathan and his armor-bearer are missing.
Saul asks Ahiah to bring the ark — or, as the Greek Septuagint reads, the ephod — in order to consult God.

f.g: The Septuagint reads “ephod,” which fits the priest's role of inquiring of the Lord here.

n: While Saul is consulting the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp grows louder. Impatient, Saul tells the priest to stop — once again, he doesn't wait on the Lord.

f.g: Stop what you are doing — probably stop drawing out the Urim and Thummim.

n: Saul's army rushes into battle and finds the Philistines in total confusion, attacking each other with their own swords.

f.w: every man's sword was against his fellow

f.g: confusion, panic

n: Hebrews who had been serving with the Philistines switch sides and join Saul and Jonathan.
Israelites who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim also come out and join the pursuit once the Philistines flee.
The narrator gives credit where it belongs: the Lord saved Israel that day.

f.w: So the LORD saved Israel that day

n: But Saul had made a rash oath, forbidding his soldiers to eat until evening so he could take revenge. Exhausted and hungry, the army suffers. Notice his focus: “that I may be avenged.”

f.g: put under an oath

n: The army comes into a forest where wild honey lies on the ground.
The honey is flowing, but no one dares eat because they fear the curse of Saul's oath.
Jonathan, who never heard the oath, dips his staff in a honeycomb and eats. Immediately he is refreshed — his eyes brighten with renewed energy.

f.g: his eyes brightened; he was refreshed and revived

n: A soldier tells Jonathan about his father's strict oath and notes how faint the army has become.

f.g: strictly

n: Jonathan openly says his father has brought trouble on the land, pointing to how much a little honey refreshed him.
Jonathan reasons that if the soldiers had eaten freely of the captured food, the victory would have been even greater. Saul's oath hurt his own cause.

f.g: perhaps, by chance

n: The army pursues the Philistines all the way from Michmash to Aijalon, about twenty miles, and ends up completely exhausted.
At evening the starving soldiers rush on the captured animals and eat the meat with the blood still in it, breaking God's law.

f.w: did eat them with the blood

n: When Saul hears of it, he calls it a sin and orders a large stone rolled over to use as a proper place to slaughter animals and drain the blood.

f.g: You have acted faithlessly.

n: Saul sends word for everyone to bring their animals to the stone and slaughter them properly, and the people obey that night.
Saul builds an altar to the Lord, his first. The narrator's note may hint that Saul's devotion was late in coming.

f.g: Or “he began to build it as an altar”; the Hebrew is ambiguous.

n: Saul wants to pursue the Philistines all night. The people agree, but the priest wisely suggests first seeking God's direction.

f.w: Let us draw near hither unto God

n: Saul asks God whether to attack, but receives no answer that day — a sign something is wrong.
Saul calls the leaders together to find out what sin has caused God's silence.

f.g: Literally “corners,” meaning leaders.

n: Saul swears that the guilty person must die, even if it is his own son Jonathan. The people, knowing what Jonathan did, remain silent.
Saul divides the group: the people on one side, himself and Jonathan on the other, to determine the guilty party by lot.
Saul prays for a clear answer, and the lot falls on Saul and Jonathan rather than the people.

f.g: The Greek version suggests a prayer using the Urim and Thummim to show the truth.

n: Lots are cast between Saul and Jonathan, and Jonathan is chosen.
Jonathan confesses honestly: he only tasted a little honey on the end of his staff — and for that he must die?
Saul, stubbornly bound to his rash vow, declares that Jonathan must die. His pride in keeping his word outweighs mercy and good sense.

f.w: God do so and more also
f.g: an oath: may God punish me severely if I do not do this

n: The people intervene: the man through whom God won this great victory will not die! They swear not a hair of his head will be harmed, and they rescue him.

f.w: there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground

f.g: he has worked together with God

n: Saul calls off the pursuit, and the Philistines return home. The chance for complete victory slips away.
This summary shows Saul's military success. He fights enemies on all sides — Moab, Ammon, Edom, Zobah, and the Philistines — and harasses them wherever he goes.

f.g: An Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Israel.
harassed, troubled; some versions read “was victorious.”

n: Saul also strikes the Amalekites, longtime enemies who raided Israel — setting up chapter 15.
Saul's children are listed. Jonathan we know; Ishui is likely Abinadab; and Saul's daughters Merab and Michal will both be promised to David.
Saul's wife Ahinoam and his army commander Abner, his cousin, are named. Abner will play a major role after Saul's death.
A brief family tree: Kish (Saul's father) and Ner (Abner's father) were both sons of Abiel.
War with the Philistines continues throughout Saul's reign. Whenever Saul sees a strong, brave man, he drafts him into service — which is how David will enter his court.
